title: In re National Football League Players’ Concussion Injury Litigation — preliminary approval denied
lead: The first proposed professional-football concussion settlement offered substantial but capped funds over decades. The court withheld preliminary approval until it could examine the financial analyses supporting promised benefits.

actors.name: Retired National Football League players and related claimants
National Football League and NFL Properties

proceedings: Player suits began July 2011 and were consolidated for pretrial proceedings.
2013 mediation produced principal terms; motion filed January 6, 2014.
January 14 order denied preliminary approval and certification without prejudice, requesting financial documentation.
limits: Original capped proposal only, distinct from later uncapped settlement and appeals. No certified class, final approval, liability finding, actuarial determination of ten-percent illness, or collusion finding.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Players allege concealed neurological risks
paragraphs: Beginning in July 2011, retired professional football players sued the National Football League and NFL Properties, alleging failure to protect them from chronic concussive and subconcussive injury and concealment of those risks. More than 4,500 former players filed similar cases, consolidated for pretrial proceedings before District Judge Anita Brody in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania. Riddell equipment defendants were also sued but did not join this settlement proposal.

Brody directed July 2013 mediation before retired federal judge Layn Phillips. The parties consulted medical, actuarial, and economic experts and signed principal terms in August. In December Brody appointed Perry Golkin as Special Master to examine financial arrangements. Plaintiffs filed the proposed class complaint and settlement motion January 6, 2014, without opposition from the settling defendants.

sections.title: The proposal exchanges broad releases for capped programs
paragraphs: The proposed class included retired players, representatives of deceased or incapacitated players, and derivative family-related claimants. League records indicated over twenty thousand members. One subclass lacked a qualifying diagnosis before proposed approval; another included diagnosed players and specified deceased-player representatives, including postmortem chronic traumatic encephalopathy diagnoses. This was a proposed definition, not certification.

The league parties would pay $760 million over twenty years: $75 million neurological assessment and related benefits, $675 million monetary awards, and $10 million education and prevention. Maximum awards ranged from $1.5 million early dementia to $3 million moderate dementia, $3.5 million Alzheimer’s or Parkinson’s disease, $5 million amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and $4 million death with chronic traumatic encephalopathy. Age, seasons, and offsets could reduce them. A potential further $37.5 million for shortfalls did not remove the cap.

Up to $4 million notice expense and $112.5 million fees and costs were additional. Claim administration and part of the Special Master’s expense nevertheless came from the monetary fund. Members would release claims, dismiss actions, and promise not to sue specified parties. Monetary recipients additionally had to abandon or refrain from cognitive-injury litigation against collegiate, amateur, and youth organizations, including the National Collegiate Athletic Association.

sections.title: Agreement does not replace scrutiny of absent members’ interests
paragraphs: Brody explained that preliminary approval was less demanding than final approval but still asked whether obvious defects existed and whether the bargain fell within a potentially fair range. The court had to compare benefits with expected recovery. Once counsel and defendants agreed, ordinary adversarial testing could weaken while absent members remained bound by releases. Settlement before certification therefore required particular care, and finding obvious defects before notice avoided futile expense.

Final approval would examine litigation risks, cost and duration, reaction, discovery, defendants’ resources, and recovery ranges. But this was not that final inquiry. A settlement class also had to satisfy certification requirements independently. Because another deficiency was sufficient, Brody did not decide conditional certification.

sections.title: Financial conclusions arrive without their supporting analyses
sections.cue: The motion is denied without prejudice
paragraphs: Brody saw no indication of bad faith or bargaining other than at arm’s length. She nevertheless could not determine whether every eligible player would receive promised benefits before the fund depleted. A sixty-five-year award program, about twenty thousand potential members, and large diagnostic awards demanded support. Even a hypothetical ten-percent diagnosis rate raised questions; she did not find that exact rate probable or depletion certain.

Counsel and Phillips relied on expert projections, but the actual analyses were not supplied. Assurances could not enable the judge and Special Master to test the proposal. Concerns also remained about assessment benefits and releases benefiting amateur organizations, so financial projections alone might not settle every issue.

On January 14, 2014 Brody denied preliminary approval and class certification without prejudice and directed submission of financial documentation through the Special Master as the first step toward possible approval. She neither required an uncapped settlement as the only lawful design nor found collusion or league liability. No class was certified and no settlement finally approved at this stage.
